edges/21.description: Anterior pituitary dysfunction can include growth hormone deficiency.

edges/22.description: Anterior pituitary dysfunction can include thyroid hormone deficiency.

edges/23.description: Pituitary dysfunction can be accompanied by reduced pituitary size on MRI.

edges/24.description: Chorioretinal degeneration manifests as chorioretinal dystrophy.

edges/25.description: Progressive chorioretinal degeneration produces chorioretinal atrophy.

edges/26.description: Progressive retinal degeneration includes RPE atrophy.

edges/28.description: Peripheral axonal degeneration manifests as axonal neuropathy.

edges/29.description: Peripheral axonal neuropathy can manifest as reduced tendon reflexes.

evidence.snippet: Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome (BNS, MIM 215470) is a rare autosomal recessive syndrome caused by mutations in the PNPLA6 gene.
evidence.explanation: Directly identifies PNPLA6 as the causal gene for BNS.

evidence.snippet: both mutations (one novel and one known) fell in the phospholipase esterase domain, where most pathogenic mutations seem to cluster
evidence.explanation: Documents that pathogenic PNPLA6 variants in BNS cluster in the phospholipase esterase (catalytic) domain.

evidence.snippet: A wide spectrum of neurodegenerative diseases has been associated with pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 (patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing protein 6) gene, including spastic paraplegia type 39, Gordon-Holmes, Boucher-Neuhauser, Oliver-Mc Farlane, and Laurence-Moon syndromes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes BNS as part of the broader allelic PNPLA6 disorder spectrum.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) pathogenic variants in PNPLA6 (19p13.2), encoding neuropathy target esterase, cause BNS. Reported variants are predominantly missense, with frameshift, splice-altering, and nonsense variants also described; missense/in-frame variants are enriched in the catalytic phospholipase/esterase (patatin-like) domain. PNPLA6 is also the cause of allelic disorders on the same spectrum, including Gordon Holmes syndrome, Oliver-McFarlane syndrome, Laurence-Moon syndrome, and spastic paraplegia type 39.

evidence.snippet: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Hormone replacement therapy at the expected time of puberty.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends hormone replacement therapy for the hypogonadotropic hypogonadism of PNPLA6 disorders.

treatments/0.description: Management is symptomatic. Hormone replacement therapy is given for the endocrine deficiencies: at the expected time of puberty for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, during childhood/adolescence for growth hormone deficiency, and as soon as identified for hypothyroidism.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replaces deficient sex-hormone signaling at the expected time of puberty.

treatments/0/targets/1.description: Replaces deficient growth or thyroid hormone when indicated.

evidence.snippet: Management is symptomatic and individually tailored. Ataxia. Continuous training of speech and swallowing, fine-motor skills, gait, and balance.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes the symptomatic, multidisciplinary supportive management of PNPLA6 disorders.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Alcohol; obesity; inactive, sedentary lifestyle; exposure to medications or chemicals that exacerbate neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists agents/circumstances to avoid, captured here as part of supportive management guidance.

treatments/1.description: Symptomatic, individually tailored multidisciplinary care: continuous training of speech/swallowing, fine-motor skills, gait, and balance for ataxia; physical therapy, assistive walking devices, and antispasticity measures for spasticity; and low-vision aids and visual rehabilitation for chorioretinal dystrophy. Patients should avoid alcohol, obesity, a sedentary lifestyle, and medications/chemicals that exacerbate neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Once the PNPLA6 pathogenic variants in the family have been identified, carrier testing for at-risk relatives, prenatal testing for a pregnancy at increased risk, and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes the genetic-counseling options available for PNPLA6 disorders.

treatments/2.description: Genetic counseling is recommended given autosomal recessive inheritance. Once the familial PNPLA6 variants are known, carrier testing for at-risk relatives, prenatal testing, and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.

evidence.snippet: Boucher-Neuhäuser and Gordon Holmes syndromes in fact represent phenotypic clusters on a spectrum of neurodegenerative diseases caused by mutations in PNPLA6.
evidence.explanation: The 2014 spectrum paper states the disease-boundary issue directly.

open_questions/0.rationale: The triad remains clinically useful, but PNPLA6 case series increasingly show overlapping retinal, endocrine, cerebellar, pyramidal, and peripheral nerve features across named syndromes. Overcommitting to a rigid syndrome boundary would understate this allelic continuum.

evidence.snippet: We used recombinant C6ST-1 to show that the identified missense mutation completely abolishes C6ST-1 activity.
evidence.explanation: Direct enzymatic demonstration that the disease allele eliminates C6ST-1 catalytic function.

evidence.snippet: Wild-type recombinant C6ST-1 showed a typical Golgi localization
evidence.explanation: Establishes the Golgi as the subcellular compartment in which C6ST-1 acts.

steps/1.description: Biallelic pathogenic CHST3 variants abolish or severely reduce the activity of carbohydrate sulfotransferase 3 (chondroitin 6-O-sulfotransferase-1), a Golgi enzyme that transfers sulfate from PAPS to the C-6 position of N-acetylgalactosamine residues in chondroitin. Missense alleles in the PAPS-binding site abolish activity outright; other alleles are hypomorphic and retain partial activity, which may contribute to the observed phenotypic breadth.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans in dermal fibroblasts showed markedly decreased 6-O-sulfation but enhanced 4-O-sulfation, confirming functional impairment of CHST3 and distinguishing them from diastrophic dysplasia sulphate transporter (DTDST)-deficient cells.
evidence.explanation: Documents the reciprocal 6-O-/4-O-sulfation shift and its diagnostic specificity versus DTDST deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Our results indicate that the mutation in CHST3 described here causes a specific but generalized defect of CS chain sulfation resulting in chondrodysplasia with major involvement of the spine.
evidence.explanation: States the causal link from the sulfation defect to chondrodysplasia with predominant spinal involvement.

steps/2.description: Absent or reduced C6ST-1 activity produces a specific but generalized defect of chondroitin sulfate chain sulfation: 6-O-sulfated disaccharides are markedly depleted while 4-O-sulfated disaccharides are relatively increased, with appearance of a disulfated 4,6-species that is undetectable in controls. The defect is demonstrable in patient dermal fibroblasts and in urine, and distinguishes CHST3 deficiency from the global undersulfation of SLC26A2 (DTDST) deficiency.

evidence.snippet: This enzyme mediates the sulfation of proteoglycans, particularly chondroitin sulfate (CS), in the extracellular matrix of cartilage.
evidence.explanation: Places the enzymatic defect in the cartilage extracellular matrix compartment.

evidence.snippet: Carbohydrate sulfotransferases (CHST) catalyse the biosynthesis of proteoglycans that enable physical interactions and signalling between different neighbouring cells in physiological and pathological states.
evidence.explanation: Review evidence that CHST-dependent proteoglycan sulfation underlies cell-matrix physical interaction and signalling.

steps/3.description: Chondroitin sulfate chains carried on cartilage proteoglycans determine the fixed charge density, hydration and growth-factor-binding behaviour of the extracellular matrix. Loss of 6-O-sulfation alters these physical and signalling properties, degrading the ability of chondrocytes to build a competent proteoglycan-rich matrix in hyaline, articular, epiphyseal and vertebral cartilage.

evidence.snippet: The most useful radiographic clues were the changes of the lumbar vertebrae.
evidence.explanation: Identifies vertebral cartilage/bone change as the cardinal radiographic manifestation of the underlying cartilage dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: All patients had spondyloepiphyseal changes that were progressive with age
evidence.explanation: Documents progressive spondyloepiphyseal involvement in a 14-patient series.

steps/4.description: Impaired matrix assembly in growth-plate, epiphyseal and vertebral cartilage produces prenatal-onset growth deficiency, epiphyseal dysplasia, flared metaphyses, and characteristic vertebral changes (lumbar vertebral clefting and widened interpedicular distances early; platyspondyly and progressive spinal deformity later). Radiographic vertebral change is the most useful diagnostic clue.

evidence.snippet: their clinical features included congenital dislocation of the knees, elbow joint dysplasia with subluxation and limited extension, hip dysplasia or dislocation, clubfoot, short stature, and kyphoscoliosis developing in late childhood
evidence.explanation: Describes the congenital dislocation pattern together with the elbow joint dysplasia that indicates a structural rather than purely ligamentous lesion.

evidence.snippet: bifid distal ends of humeri which can be considered a diagnostic key in patients with CHST3 variants
evidence.explanation: Structural malformation of the distal humerus supports primary joint dysplasia as the basis of the radial-head dislocation.

steps/5.description: Dislocation of the knees, hips and radial heads is present at birth and is interpreted as primary dysplasia of the joint structures themselves rather than generalized ligamentous laxity — the joint surfaces and distal humeri are radiographically malformed (bifid distal humerus with radial head subluxation). Club feet accompany the dislocations.

evidence.snippet: Minor heart valve dysplasia has been described in several persons.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents recurrent valve dysplasia across unrelated persons.

evidence.snippet: Echocardiography in seven affected individuals revealed multiple heart valve anomalies
evidence.explanation: Multivalvular involvement in all echocardiographed members of a large CHST3 kindred establishes valve tissue as a disease site.

evidence.snippet: it reinforces that lethal cardiac involvement is a critical clinical finding of the disorder.
evidence.explanation: Documents that cardiac involvement can be lethal, which motivates the echocardiographic surveillance recommendation. The abstract does not name the lethal lesion, so this supports the node as a surveillance target rather than establishing that valve dysplasia is the lethal lesion.

steps/6.description: Dysplasia of the cardiac valve leaflets with mitral, tricuspid and/or aortic regurgitation occurs in a minority of patients. Reported valve involvement is clinically minor; lethal cardiac involvement has separately been reported in a CHST3 series without the responsible lesion being specified, and it is that unattributed lethality — not the valve dysplasia itself — that motivates echocardiographic surveillance. Valve leaflets are proteoglycan-rich connective tissue and the C6ST-1 substrate (chondroitin-bearing proteoglycan) is a general connective-tissue constituent, but CHST3-deficient valve tissue has never been examined directly, so the step from deficient 6-O-sulfation to valve dysplasia is uncharacterized.

evidence.snippet: short stature, and progressive kyphosis developing in late childhood
evidence.explanation: Documents the progressive spinal course after the congenital presentation.

evidence.snippet: Progressive joint pain and movement restriction are the main characteristics of CHST3-related skeletal dysplasia.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review of published cases identifies progressive arthropathy as the dominant clinical feature.

evidence.snippet: We describe a family with progressive skeletal dysplasia and severe spinal involvement, short stature, premature arthrosis and joint contractures
evidence.explanation: Independent family confirming premature arthrosis and contracture development.

steps/7.description: Beyond the congenital malformation, the abnormal matrix degenerates progressively: joint pain, premature arthrosis, contractures and increasing limitation of range of motion accumulate, and kyphosis or kyphoscoliosis develops in late childhood and worsens. This progressive arm, not the neonatal dislocations, drives most long-term disability.

evidence.snippet: Chondrodysplasia with congenital joint dislocations, CHST3-related (CDCJD-CHST3) is characterized by short stature of prenatal onset, joint dislocations (knees, hips, radial heads), clubfeet, and limitation of range of motion that can involve all large joints.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists large-joint dislocation as a defining characteristic, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: We report eight CHST3 mutations in six unrelated individuals who presented at birth with congenital joint dislocations.
evidence.explanation: All six molecularly confirmed probands presented at birth with congenital dislocations (6/6), consistent with a VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/8.description: Dislocation of the large joints — most consistently the knees, hips and radial heads — present at birth. This is the defining presenting feature and the reason affected infants were historically diagnosed with Larsen syndrome or humero-spinal dysostosis.

evidence.snippet: Her half-brother presented at birth with bilateral knee dislocation and talipes equinovarus.
evidence.explanation: Direct clinical description of congenital bilateral knee dislocation.

steps/9.description: Dislocation of the knee, frequently bilateral and apparent in the neonatal period, sometimes with genu recurvatum.

evidence.snippet: hip dysplasia or dislocation
evidence.explanation: Hip involvement documented in the defining CHST3 cohort.

steps/10.description: Hip dysplasia or frank dislocation, present congenitally in a majority but not all affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: joint dislocations (knees, hips, radial heads)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names the radial head among the characteristically dislocated joints.

steps/11.description: Radial head dislocation or subluxation accompanied by dysplasia of the distal humerus, with limited elbow extension. Highly characteristic of the CHST3 phenotype.

evidence.snippet: elbow joint dysplasia with subluxation and limited extension
evidence.explanation: Explicit description of restricted elbow extension in the CHST3 cohort.

steps/12.description: Elbow joint dysplasia with subluxation and restricted extension, a consistent finding across CHST3 series.

evidence.snippet: bifid distal ends of humeri which can be considered a diagnostic key in patients with CHST3 variants
evidence.explanation: All 14 patients in this series had bifid distal humeri, proposed as a diagnostic key.

steps/13.description: Bifid or notched distal humeral end on radiographs, proposed as a near-pathognomonic radiographic clue for CHST3 variants.

evidence.snippet: joint dislocations (knees, hips, radial heads), clubfeet, and limitation of range of motion that can involve all large joints
evidence.explanation: Clubfeet listed by GeneReviews among the features the disorder is characterized by, mapping to the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: talipes equinovarus
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation of congenital talipes equinovarus.

steps/14.description: Bilateral talipes equinovarus, present at birth in essentially all reported patients.

evidence.snippet: is characterized by short stature of prenatal onset
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists prenatal-onset short stature as a defining feature, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: In the systematic review, short stature, limited joint extension, joint pain, and joint dislocation were the most common characteristics of this disorder.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review of all published cases ranks short stature among the most common features.

steps/15.description: Disproportionate short stature beginning before birth, with reduced birth length and persistent short-trunk short stature; adult height is severely reduced.

evidence.snippet: limitation of range of motion that can involve all large joints
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews includes limitation of range of motion in the defining characterization, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/16.description: Restricted movement affecting all large joints, progressive with age and a principal contributor to functional disability.

evidence.snippet: short stature, and progressive kyphosis developing in late childhood
evidence.explanation: A 24-patient series reports progressive kyphosis among the shared features of the group, mapping to the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Kyphosis and occasionally scoliosis with slight shortening of the trunk develop in childhood.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms childhood-onset kyphosis.

steps/17.description: Thoracic kyphosis appearing in childhood and worsening thereafter, with slight shortening of the trunk.

evidence.snippet: kyphoscoliosis developing in late childhood
evidence.explanation: Direct clinical description of kyphoscoliosis in the CHST3 cohort.

steps/18.description: Combined kyphosis and scoliosis developing in late childhood in a subset of patients.

evidence.snippet: Kyphosis and occasionally scoliosis with slight shortening of the trunk develop in childhood.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews qualifies scoliosis as occurring occasionally, which maps to the OCCASIONAL band (5-29%).

steps/19.description: Scoliosis occurring in a minority of patients, developing during childhood.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic variants in CHST3 gene result in congenital dislocation of large joints, club feet, short stature, rhizomelia, kypho-scoliosis, platyspondyly, epiphyseal dysplasia, flared metaphysis, in addition to minor cardiac lesions and hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: Platyspondyly is listed among the core radiographic manifestations.

steps/20.description: Flattened vertebral bodies, part of the spondyloepiphyseal radiographic pattern.

evidence.snippet: All patients had spondyloepiphyseal changes that were progressive with age
evidence.explanation: Progressive epiphyseal involvement documented in all 14 patients.

steps/21.description: Irregular, dysplastic epiphyses that become more evident with age, part of the spondyloepiphyseal pattern.

evidence.snippet: short stature, rhizomelia, kypho-scoliosis, platyspondyly, epiphyseal dysplasia, flared metaphysis
evidence.explanation: Flared metaphysis listed among the skeletal manifestations of biallelic CHST3 variants.

steps/22.description: Metaphyseal flaring of the long bones on skeletal survey.

evidence.snippet: congenital dislocation of large joints, club feet, short stature, rhizomelia
evidence.explanation: Rhizomelia listed among the core manifestations.

steps/23.description: Disproportionate shortening of the proximal limb segments.

evidence.snippet: congenital joint (knee and elbow) dislocations, short trunk short stature progressive vertebral anomalies, and metacarpal shortening
evidence.explanation: Metacarpal shortening reported as a key symptom in nine Indian patients.

evidence.snippet: metacarpal shortening and accessory carpal ossification centers
evidence.explanation: Independent extension of the Omani-type phenotype to include metacarpal shortening.

steps/24.description: Shortening of the metacarpals, developing over time and contributing to a brachydactyly-like hand appearance.

evidence.snippet: metacarpal shortening and accessory carpal ossification centers
evidence.explanation: Direct documentation of accessory carpal ossification centers.

evidence.snippet: supernumerary carpal ossification centers
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation in an Indian cohort.

steps/25.description: Supernumerary carpal ossification centers on hand radiographs. Carpal bone age remains normal, which helps separate CHST3 deficiency from Desbuquois dysplasia (advanced carpal ossification).

evidence.snippet: short stature, premature arthrosis and joint contractures
evidence.explanation: Direct clinical description of premature arthrosis with contractures.

steps/26.description: Early degenerative arthropathy with contractures, producing pain and increasing functional limitation from childhood onward.

evidence.snippet: Progressive joint pain and movement restriction are the main characteristics of CHST3-related skeletal dysplasia.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review conclusion naming progressive joint pain as a main characteristic.

steps/27.description: Aggravating joint pain, identified by systematic review of published cases as one of the main features of the disorder in older children and adults.

evidence.snippet: Minor heart valve dysplasia has been described in several persons.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes valve dysplasia in several persons rather than as a defining feature, mapping to the OCCASIONAL band.

evidence.snippet: Echocardiography showed abnormal cardiac valves.
evidence.explanation: Independent echocardiographic confirmation of valve involvement.

evidence.snippet: it reinforces that lethal cardiac involvement is a critical clinical finding of the disorder.
evidence.explanation: Source for the lethal cardiac course referred to in this description. Graded PARTIAL because the abstract attributes the lethality to cardiac involvement in general and never names the valve as the responsible lesion; the only cardiac lesion it enumerates is atrial septal defect, listed among rare unusual associated findings.

steps/28.description: Minor dysplasia of the cardiac valves with mitral, tricuspid and/or aortic regurgitation. The reported valve involvement is clinically minor. A lethal cardiac course has been reported separately, without the responsible lesion being specified, and echocardiographic surveillance is recommended on that basis rather than on the severity of the valve dysplasia itself.

evidence.snippet: affected members of this family also had cardiac involvement including mitral, tricuspid and/or aortic regurgitations and type E brachydactyly
evidence.explanation: Documents multivalvular regurgitation in CHST3 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Mitral valve regurgitation and tricuspid valve regurgitation was observed in all patients.
evidence.explanation: Independent kindred confirming multivalvular regurgitation; mitral and tricuspid regurgitation were present in all echocardiographed affected individuals.

steps/29.description: Valvular regurgitation involving the mitral, tricuspid and/or aortic valves, described in an affected Turkish family with a hypomorphic CHST3 allele and in a large Pakistani kindred, in which mitral and tricuspid regurgitation were present in every affected individual examined by echocardiography.

evidence.snippet: broad forehead, broad nasal tip, long philtrum and short neck
evidence.explanation: Short neck documented as part of the shared phenotype.

steps/30.description: Short neck accompanying the short-trunk body habitus.

evidence.snippet: He was found to have vertebral artery stenosis secondary to atlantoaxial instability (AAI) due to an os odontoideum.
evidence.explanation: Single case report; the authors state it is a previously unreported complication, supporting the VERY_RARE band.

steps/31.description: Atlantoaxial instability due to an os odontoideum, complicated in a reported case by vertebral artery stenosis and posterior circulation ischaemic stroke, treated with occipitocervical fusion. Described as a previously unreported complication and therefore not an established recurrent feature, but clinically important because it is catastrophic and surgically treatable.

edges/1.description: Loss of enzyme activity directly removes the 6-O-sulfation step of chondroitin sulfate chain maturation.

edges/2.description: Undersulfated chondroitin sulfate chains alter the charge density and interaction profile of cartilage proteoglycans.

evidence.snippet: C6ST-1 catalyzes sulfation of chondroitin containing proteoglycan, an essential constituent of connective tissues
evidence.explanation: Supports the premise that the enzyme's substrate is a general connective-tissue constituent rather than cartilage-specific; the paper does not examine valve tissue, so the edge is marked indirect with unknown intermediates.

edges/3.description: Cardiac valve leaflets are proteoglycan-rich connective tissue, so undersulfated chondroitin chains are presumed to compromise the valve matrix, but CHST3-deficient valve tissue has not been examined and the intervening steps are unknown.

edges/4.description: A defective proteoglycan matrix impairs the organization and biomechanical competence of growth-plate and epiphyseal cartilage.

edges/5.description: Malformed articular surfaces, rather than simple ligamentous laxity, produce dislocation of the large joints at birth.

edges/6.description: An intrinsically abnormal cartilage matrix degenerates under normal mechanical loading over years, with abnormal joint alignment adding chronic aberrant loading.

edges/7.description: Failure of growth-plate cartilage to sustain normal endochondral growth produces growth deficiency that begins before birth and persists.

edges/8.description: Dysplasia of vertebral body cartilage produces flattened vertebral bodies.

edges/9.description: Impaired matrix assembly in epiphyseal cartilage produces irregular, dysplastic epiphyses that become more evident with age.

edges/10.description: Disordered growth-plate remodelling produces metaphyseal flaring of the long bones.

edges/11.description: Growth failure at the proximal long-bone growth plates shortens the proximal limb segments disproportionately.

edges/12.description: Growth failure of the tubular bones of the hand produces progressive metacarpal shortening.

edges/13.description: Disordered endochondral ossification of the carpal cartilage anlagen produces supernumerary ossification centers while carpal bone age remains normal.

edges/14.description: Cervical vertebral involvement in the generalized vertebral cartilage dysplasia is inferred to shorten the neck along with the trunk. The source lists short neck within the facial gestalt sentence rather than tying it to vertebral shortening, so the intermediate step is inferred from the short-trunk habitus and is not directly evidenced.

evidence.snippet: AAI due to an os odontoideum is a previously unreported complication of CHST3-related skeletal dysplasia.
evidence.explanation: The case report attributes the atlantoaxial instability to an os odontoideum arising as a complication of the underlying skeletal dysplasia; this is a single case, so the edge rests on that attribution.

edges/15.description: Dysplastic ossification of the odontoid process can produce an os odontoideum, whose incompetent dens destabilizes the atlantoaxial articulation.

edges/16.description: Malformed articular surfaces dislocate under normal intrauterine loading, so the large-joint dislocations are present at birth.

edges/17.description: Dysplasia of the knee joint produces congenital, frequently bilateral, knee dislocation.

edges/18.description: Dysplasia of the hip joint produces congenital hip dysplasia or frank dislocation.

edges/19.description: Malformation of the distal humerus and proximal radius produces radial head dislocation or subluxation.

edges/20.description: The malformed distal humeral articular structure is seen radiographically as a bifid or notched distal humeral end.

edges/21.description: Elbow joint dysplasia with subluxation mechanically restricts extension from birth.

edges/22.description: Congenital dysplasia of the foot and ankle joints produces talipes equinovarus, which accompanies the large-joint dislocations.

edges/23.description: Degeneration of intrinsically abnormal articular cartilage under normal loading produces early arthrosis with contractures.

edges/24.description: Progressive degenerative arthropathy is experienced as aggravating joint pain from childhood onward.

edges/25.description: Accumulating arthrosis and contracture progressively restrict movement of the large joints, on top of the congenital restriction from joint dysplasia.

edges/26.description: Progressive deformation of dysplastic vertebral and intervertebral structures produces childhood-onset, worsening kyphosis.

edges/27.description: Combined progressive sagittal and coronal spinal deformity develops in late childhood in a subset of patients.

edges/28.description: Coronal-plane spinal deformity develops during childhood in a minority of patients.

edges/29.description: The tissue-level valve dysplasia is observed clinically as abnormal valve morphology on echocardiography.

edges/30.description: Dysplastic valve leaflets fail to coapt, producing regurgitation across the affected valves.

evidence.snippet: We sequenced candidate genes from the region and identified a missense mutation in the chondroitin 6-O-sulfotransferase (C6ST-1) gene (CHST3)
evidence.explanation: Original gene identification by linkage mapping in two consanguineous Omani families.

evidence.snippet: We report eight CHST3 mutations in six unrelated individuals who presented at birth with congenital joint dislocations.
evidence.explanation: Establishes CHST3 as the cause of the congenital-dislocation phenotype in unrelated probands previously labelled recessive Larsen syndrome or humero-spinal dysostosis.

evidence.snippet: All these variants are located on sulfotransferase domain of CHST3 protein and were classified as pathogenic/ likely pathogenic.
evidence.explanation: Supports clustering of pathogenic alleles in the sulfotransferase domain.

genes/0.notes: CHST3 (10q22.1, NM_004273.5) encodes carbohydrate sulfotransferase 3 / chondroitin 6-O-sulfotransferase-1, a Golgi type II membrane sulfotransferase. Reported pathogenic alleles span missense, nonsense, frameshift and splice-site classes and cluster in the sulfotransferase domain; missense alleles affecting the PAPS-binding site abolish activity, while some missense alleles are hypomorphic.

evidence.snippet: Surgical correction of the abnormal joints is the only treatment modality; however, surgical correction is often only partially successful and multiple procedures are needed.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management statement, including the caveat on limited efficacy.

treatments/0.description: Surgical correction and stabilization of the abnormal joints is the only disease-directed treatment modality available. Correction is often only partially successful and multiple procedures are typically needed. There is no approved enzyme replacement, small-molecule, gene, RNA or cell therapy for CHST3-related skeletal dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: Occipitocervical fusion yielded good clinical results with the 1-year follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Single-case evidence for surgical benefit; not generalizable to routine management.

treatments/1.description: Cervical spinal fusion is indicated when atlantoaxial instability threatens the vertebral arteries or spinal cord. In the reported case complicated by posterior circulation stroke, occipitocervical fusion produced neurological improvement and return to independent ambulation at one-year follow-up.

evidence.snippet: Physical therapy has not been effective.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews explicitly refutes efficacy of physical therapy for the joint manifestations of this disorder.

treatments/2.description: Physical therapy is used for general mobility support, but GeneReviews explicitly notes that it has not been effective for the joint manifestations of this disorder. It is recorded here with that negative qualification so the entry does not overstate benefit.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Activities with a high impact on joints (e.g., jogging) and obesity.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews Agents/Circumstances to Avoid recommendation.

treatments/3.description: High-impact activity (for example jogging) and obesity should be avoided because of the intrinsically abnormal joint cartilage and the progressive degenerative course.

evidence.snippet: Clinical joint and spine evaluation with orthopedist with experience in skeletal dysplasia; radiographs as recommended per orthopedist
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance recommendation.

treatments/4.description: Ongoing joint and spine evaluation by an orthopedist experienced in skeletal dysplasia, radiographs as recommended, cardiology follow-up with periodic echocardiography, and annual dental review.

evidence.snippet: Once the CHST3 pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk family members and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing for a pregnancy at increased risk are possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews genetic counseling guidance.

treatments/5.description: Autosomal recessive recurrence counseling (25% affected, 50% carrier, 25% unaffected non-carrier per pregnancy for heterozygous parents), carrier testing for at-risk relatives, and prenatal or preimplantation genetic testing once the familial CHST3 variants are known.

open_questions/0.rationale: The biochemical lesion (6-O-sulfation loss with compensatory 4-O-sulfation) and the clinical outcome (primary joint dysplasia with congenital dislocation) are both well documented, but the intervening cell-biological step is not. No CHST3-specific growth-plate study, patient-derived chondrocyte or cartilage organoid model, or quantitative Chst3-null skeletal phenotype has been published; all direct functional evidence comes from dermal fibroblasts and recombinant enzyme assays, which cannot reproduce the biomechanical environment of cartilage.

evidence.snippet: There is no apparent genotype-phenotype correlation in this disorder.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review finding that motivates the genotype-phenotype arm of this knowledge gap.

open_questions/1.rationale: Published evidence consists of small retrospective series. No prospective natural-history registry, validated phenotype frequency, prevalence or carrier-frequency estimate, standardized functional endpoint, or patient-reported outcome measure exists, and a systematic review of the published cases found no apparent genotype-phenotype correlation despite the coexistence of null and hypomorphic alleles.

open_questions/2.rationale: Valve involvement recurs across unrelated kindreds, and lethal cardiac involvement has been reported in one series without the responsible lesion being identified, so whether the deaths are valvular is itself unresolved. Valve leaflets are proteoglycan-rich connective tissue, but no study has examined the glycosaminoglycan composition or structure of CHST3-deficient valve tissue. The ventricular and atrial septal defects have each been reported once, in different families; cardiac septation defects are not an expected consequence of a matrix-sulfation lesion, so their causal status is unresolved and no pathograph edge is asserted for them.

evidence.snippet: They also shared peculiar facies with broad forehead, broad nasal tip, long philtrum and short neck.
evidence.explanation: The sole source for the facial gestalt reports it descriptively, without any mechanistic account, which is the basis of this knowledge gap.

open_questions/3.rationale: Broad forehead and long philtrum are reported only as components of a facial gestalt observed in a single 14-patient series, with no craniofacial imaging, cranial-base measurement, or developmental study relating them to the matrix-sulfation lesion. No mechanistic literature connects them to any curated pathophysiology node, so they are deliberately left unwired rather than attached by an inferred edge. Short neck, listed in the same gestalt sentence, is wired only because the short-trunk habitus supplies a plausible named intermediate; the facial features have no comparable anchor.

evidence.snippet: The conductive portion of the hearing loss may be due to ossicular malformation; however, the sensorineural hearing loss requires further exploration.
evidence.explanation: The primary hearing-loss study itself states that the mechanism is unresolved, which is the basis of this knowledge gap.

open_questions/4.rationale: The Pakistani kindred study that established hearing loss as part of the CHST3 spectrum explicitly leaves the mechanism open, and no temporal-bone imaging or inner-ear glycosaminoglycan study has been published, so the hearing phenotype is deliberately left without a causal pathograph edge.

evidence.snippet: we have solved the solution structure of COA6, which reveals a coiled-coil-helix-coiled-coil-helix domain typical of redox-active proteins found in the mitochondrial inter-membrane space
evidence.explanation: Establishes the redox-active CHCH fold and intermembrane-space character that define this node's molecular lesion.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate that COA6 can reduce the copper-coordinating disulfides of its client proteins, SCO1 and COX2, allowing for copper binding
evidence.explanation: States the specific catalytic activity lost in this disorder, and names the two client proteins whose cysteines go unreduced.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate that COA6 acts as a thiol-reductase to reduce disulfide bridges of critical cysteine residues in SCO1 and SCO2.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation of the thiol-reductase assignment, adding SCO2 to the client set.

evidence.snippet: Strikingly, mutations in COA6 significantly skew the relative ratio of reduced to oxidized cysteinyl sulfurs of SCO1, with the oxidized species predominating (Figure 6F).
evidence.explanation: The redox defect is measured in COA6 patient-derived fibroblasts.

steps/1.description: Disease-associated COA6 variants impair protein abundance or function. Biochemical studies support a role for COA6 in reducing copper-coordinating cysteines of SCO1, SCO2 and COX2. Patient-derived fibroblasts showed a shift toward oxidized SCO1, whereas SCO2 oxidation differed between those cells and an engineered knockout model. W59C retains partial function in human complementation assays. A physiological copper-carrier role remains debated.

evidence.snippet: COA6 interacts transiently with the copper-containing catalytic domain of newly synthesized COX2.
evidence.explanation: Places COA6 physically at the COX2 copper domain, which is the site this node describes.

evidence.snippet: Our analyses define COA6 as a constituent of the mitochondrial copper relay system, linking defects in COX2 metallation to cardiac cytochrome c oxidase deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Connects failed COX2 metallation to the cardiac COX deficiency that this entry's downstream nodes describe.

evidence.snippet: Our data reveal that COA6 is intricately involved in the copper-dependent biogenesis of COX2.
evidence.explanation: Independent statement that COX2 biogenesis is copper-dependent and COA6-dependent.

steps/2.description: COA6 dysfunction compromises maturation of the binuclear CuA centre of COX2. COA6 interacts with newly synthesized COX2 and copper-delivery proteins. Reconstitution studies support transfer of Cu(I) from SCO1 to reduced COX2; the degree of failed metallation has not been directly quantified in the reported patient myocardium.

evidence.snippet: Absence of COA6 leads to fast turnover of newly synthesized COX2 and a concomitant reduction in cytochrome c oxidase levels.
evidence.explanation: The source full text identifies the turnover experiment as coa6-null yeast.

evidence.snippet: Using pulse-chase experiments, we demonstrate an increased turnover of mitochondrial encoded complex IV subunits.
evidence.explanation: Abnormal subunit turnover in cultured patient fibroblasts.

steps/3.description: COA6 loss compromises the stability of newly synthesized COX2 in yeast. Patient fibroblast experiments also identify abnormal turnover of mitochondrially encoded complex IV subunits. Pulse-chase profiles differ between studies, so reduced COX2 abundance should not be equated with a single universal degradation rate or with a primary translation defect.

evidence.snippet: The monomeric COX1 assembly intermediate accumulates.
evidence.explanation: Patient fibroblasts accumulate an early assembly intermediate.

evidence.snippet: Although monomeric complex IV is decreased in patient fibroblasts, the CI/CIII2 /CIVn -supercomplexes remain unaffected.
evidence.explanation: The same culture experiments distinguish monomeric complex IV from supercomplex-associated pools.

steps/4.description: COA6 deficiency reduces assembly of mature complex IV and permits accumulation of COX1-containing assembly intermediates. In the W66R patient fibroblasts, monomeric complex IV was decreased while the measured CI/CIII2/CIVn supercomplexes were preserved; the assembly phenotype is therefore not uniform across all enzyme pools.

evidence.snippet: We present a new pathogenic COA6 variant detected in a patient with neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and isolated complex IV deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Clinical presentation of the second reported patient.

evidence.snippet: Remarkably, only one of the patients described with COA6 mutations showed a decreased complex I activity
evidence.explanation: The discussion summarizes variable complex I involvement in the two foundational COA6 cases; both have complex IV deficiency.

steps/5.description: Reduced cytochrome c oxidase activity limits terminal electron transfer and coupled oxidative phosphorylation. Both isolated complex IV deficiency and combined complex I/IV deficiency occur among the foundational clinical reports. The original compound-heterozygous patient had cardiac enzyme defects despite normal fibroblast assays; the W66R patient had a fibroblast complex IV defect.

evidence.snippet: We present a new pathogenic COA6 variant detected in a patient with neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and isolated complex IV deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Clinical presentation of the second reported patient.

steps/6.description: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the dominant cardiac manifestation in the foundational COA6 reports. Respiratory-chain defects measured in affected heart support an association with myocardial bioenergetic dysfunction, but do not directly measure the sequence from ATP deficit to hypertrophic remodeling.

evidence.snippet: An additional patient with a W66R mutation in Coa6 suffered from neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, muscular hypotonia, and lactic acidosis with a COX defect in the fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Summarizes the W66R clinical report; this is background clinical evidence.

steps/7.description: Lactic acidosis was reported in the W66R patient. Impaired oxidative metabolism is a plausible explanation, but the clinical observation does not directly demonstrate increased glycolytic flux or identify the tissue producing excess lactate.

evidence.snippet: We present a new pathogenic COA6 variant detected in a patient with neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and isolated complex IV deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Clinical presentation of the second reported patient.

evidence.snippet: Remarkably, only one of the patients described with COA6 mutations showed a decreased complex I activity
evidence.explanation: The discussion summarizes variable complex I involvement in the two foundational COA6 cases; both have complex IV deficiency.

steps/8.description: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is reported in both foundational cases. Neonatal onset is specifically documented in the W66R patient.

evidence.snippet: An additional patient with a W66R mutation in Coa6 suffered from neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, muscular hypotonia, and lactic acidosis with a COX defect in the fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Summarizes the W66R clinical report; this is background clinical evidence.

steps/9.description: Lactic acidosis was described in the W66R patient. The available cases do not establish a population frequency.

evidence.snippet: An additional patient with a W66R mutation in Coa6 suffered from neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, muscular hypotonia, and lactic acidosis with a COX defect in the fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Summarizes the W66R clinical report; this is background clinical evidence.

steps/10.description: Muscular hypotonia was described in the W66R patient. This finding alone does not establish encephalopathy or a primary skeletal myopathy.

evidence.snippet: We present a new pathogenic COA6 variant detected in a patient with neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and isolated complex IV deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Clinical presentation of the second reported patient.

evidence.snippet: Remarkably, only one of the patients described with COA6 mutations showed a decreased complex I activity
evidence.explanation: The discussion summarizes variable complex I involvement in the two foundational COA6 cases; both have complex IV deficiency.

steps/11.description: Complex IV deficiency was found in both foundational reports, with tissue-dependent expression and variable involvement of complex I.

evidence.snippet: Our analyses define COA6 as thiol-reductase, which is essential for CuA biogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Asserts the causal step from COA6 reductase activity to CuA centre formation.

edges/1.description: Reduced availability of appropriately reduced copper-coordinating cysteines compromises CuA biogenesis.

evidence.snippet: Absence of COA6 leads to fast turnover of newly synthesized COX2 and a concomitant reduction in cytochrome c oxidase levels.
evidence.explanation: The 2015 full text measures rapid turnover of newly synthesized Cox2 in coa6-deleted yeast. It supports this mechanism without establishing identical turnover kinetics in every patient cell line.

edges/2.description: Defective maturation is associated with reduced COX2 stability in experimental systems; the kinetics vary with the model and assay.

evidence.snippet: caused by impaired biogenesis of the copper-bound mitochondrial DNA-encoded subunit COX2 and subsequent accumulation of complex IV assembly intermediates
evidence.explanation: Gene-edited human cells connect impaired COX2 biogenesis to accumulation of assembly intermediates.

edges/3.description: Loss of mature COX2 limits its incorporation into the assembled enzyme.

evidence.snippet: Complete loss of COA6 activity using gene editing in HEK293T cells resulted in a profound growth defect due to complex IV deficiency
evidence.explanation: Links COA6 loss to complex IV deficiency in a human cell model.

edges/4.description: Reduced mature enzyme abundance limits complex IV activity.

edges/5.description: Respiratory dysfunction provides a plausible route to systemic lactate accumulation; tissue-specific metabolic flux was not measured in the clinical reports.

edges/6.description: Hypotonia accompanies the biochemical disorder in the W66R patient, but its neural versus muscular origin and intervening mechanism have not been established.

evidence.snippet: A pathogenic mutation in COA6, leading to substitution of a conserved tryptophan for a cysteine residue, results in a loss of complex IV activity and cardiomyopathy.
evidence.explanation: Clinical or genetic observation summarized from the foundational patient reports; not a new clinical result in this mechanistic study.

edges/7.description: Cardiac respiratory-chain deficiency accompanies hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; the intervening remodeling mechanisms remain incompletely defined.

evidence.snippet: Using yeast coa6Δ cells, we show that conserved residues in the motif, including the residue mutated in a patient with mitochondrial disease, are essential for COA6 function, thus confirming the pathogenicity of the patient mutation.
evidence.explanation: Functional confirmation of variant pathogenicity by yeast complementation, which is the evidence that makes this gene causal rather than candidate.

evidence.snippet: we show that patient mutations in Coa6 disrupt Coa6-Cox2 interaction, providing the biochemical basis for disease pathogenesis
evidence.explanation: Gives the biochemical mechanism by which the patient alleles are pathogenic - loss of the COA6-COX2 interaction - rather than only that they fail to complement in yeast.

evidence.snippet: Disulfide-mediated oligomerization of the W59CCoa6 protein provides a structural explanation for the loss-of-function mutation.
evidence.explanation: A crystal structure of a patient allele, explaining at the protein level why the variant is loss-of-function.

evidence.snippet: An additional patient with a W66R mutation in Coa6 suffered from neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, muscular hypotonia, and lactic acidosis with a COX defect in the fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Clinical or genetic observation summarized from the foundational patient reports; not a new clinical result in this mechanistic study.

evidence.snippet: COA6/C1ORF31 is involved in cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) biogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the gene identity and its former alias C1orf31. Graded OTHER rather than HUMAN_CLINICAL: this is the abstract's opening sentence restating prior work, immediately before the paper presents its own patient, so it is background rather than this study's clinical finding.

genes/0.notes: COA6, formerly C1orf31, encodes an intermembrane-space assembly factor. The foundational cases carry W59C/E87* in compound heterozygosity or homozygous W66R. Variant names here follow the original full-length protein numbering; effects in overexpression or chimeric yeast assays do not establish a clinical severity ranking.

evidence.snippet: we show that exogenous copper supplementation completely rescues respiratory and complex IV assembly defects in yeast coa6Δ cells
evidence.explanation: The yeast result. Complete rescue here, in contrast with the partial rescue reported in patient fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: Copper supplementation shows a partial rescue of complex IV deficiency in patient fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Partial recovery in cultured patient cells; no clinical treatment outcome is established.

treatments/0.description: Copper supplementation is an experimental lead supported by complete rescue of respiratory and assembly defects in coa6-null yeast and partial rescue of complex IV deficiency in patient fibroblasts. These experiments do not establish clinical efficacy or an appropriate regimen for people with COA6 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Copper supplementation shows a partial rescue of complex IV deficiency in patient fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Partial recovery in cultured patient cells; no clinical treatment outcome is established.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Partially improves the complex IV deficit in cultured patient fibroblasts; restoration of CuA metallation was not directly quantified.

evidence.snippet: By using a candidate-based approach, we identified an investigational anticancer drug, elesclomol (ES), that rescues respiratory defects of COA6-deficient yeast cells by increasing mitochondrial copper content and restoring CcO activity.
evidence.explanation: Direct COA6 yeast rescue result; human efficacy is untested in this study.

evidence.snippet: Indeed, 100 nM ES treatment prevented pericardial edema and significantly increased the heart rate of Coa6-knockdown zebrafish embryos at 72 and 96 hpf without altering the heart rate of control embryos (SI Appendix, Fig. S8 E and F).
evidence.explanation: COA6 morphant fish showed functional and morphological rescue.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with the mechanism of action of ES, we observed that cosupplementation of 100 nM ES with 100 nM of copper resulted in 100% lethality (SI Appendix, Fig. S8B).
evidence.explanation: The experimental zebrafish combination was lethal; efficacy at one dose does not establish safety of copper coadministration.

treatments/1.description: Elesclomol restored mitochondrial copper, respiration and CcO activity in coa6-deficient yeast, including yeast expressing pathogenic human-yeast COA6 chimeras. It also reduced pericardial edema and improved heart rate in COA6 morphant zebrafish. This is preclinical evidence: the mammalian patient fibroblasts in the same study carried SCO2 variants, not COA6 variants. Toxicity depended on experimental conditions; combined elesclomol and copper at 100 nM each was lethal in zebrafish.

evidence.snippet: By using a candidate-based approach, we identified an investigational anticancer drug, elesclomol (ES), that rescues respiratory defects of COA6-deficient yeast cells by increasing mitochondrial copper content and restoring CcO activity.
evidence.explanation: Direct COA6 yeast rescue result; human efficacy is untested in this study.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Restored CcO activity in coa6-deficient yeast; this relationship is restricted to that experimental model.

treatments/2.description: Cardiac and metabolic support are general management considerations for severe mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. The cited COA6 reports do not establish an evidence-based disease-specific supportive or palliative protocol.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in COA6 have been reported in two unrelated human mitochondrial disease patients: one with compound heterozygous mutations (W59C and E87X) (Calvo et al., 2012) and the other with a homozygous missense mutation (W66R) (Baertling et al., 2015).
evidence.explanation: Biallelic genotypes support the inheritance model underlying counseling; the quoted study does not itself measure recurrence or test prenatal diagnosis.

treatments/3.description: For parents who each carry a pathogenic COA6 allele, standard autosomal recessive inheritance gives a 25 percent probability of a child inheriting both alleles in each pregnancy. Identification of familial variants permits discussion of carrier and reproductive testing.

open_questions/0.rationale: The cited foundational cases support a predominantly cardiac disorder, with hypotonia in one patient. They do not establish a specific encephalopathy phenotype. Sparse clinical ascertainment and infantile death leave the neurological spectrum uncertain; the disease name is not evidence for a particular CNS manifestation.

evidence.snippet: While two decades of studies have provided a clearer picture regarding the biochemical roles of SCO1 and SCO2 proteins, some discrepancy exists regarding the function of COA6, the new member of this pathway.
evidence.explanation: A critical review of the pathway stating that the question is open, which is the basis for recording it rather than asserting one side.

evidence.snippet: Its role as a copper metallochaperone has also been proposed.
evidence.explanation: Names the competing reading directly.

evidence.snippet: COA6 has the capacity to bind copper
evidence.explanation: Direct experimental support for the copper-binding side, from a paper this entry also cites for the reductase-dependent assembly defect.

evidence.snippet: the first 2 helices tethered by disulfide bonds, one of which likely provides the copper-binding site
evidence.explanation: The crystal structure assigns a likely copper-binding site, which is the structural basis for the metallochaperone proposal.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, the source of electrons used by COA6 for its disulfide reductase activity is unknown.
evidence.explanation: The review identifies an unresolved component of the reductase model.

open_questions/1.rationale: Purified COA6 can bind copper under selected in-vitro conditions, but direct physiological copper transfer from COA6 to a client protein has not been demonstrated in the studies assessed by the 2022 review. Reductase activity has stronger experimental support. Its electron source, substrate specificity and the identity of the redox-active disulfide remain incompletely resolved.

evidence.snippet: Remarkably, only one of the patients described with COA6 mutations showed a decreased complex I activity
evidence.explanation: The discussion summarizes variable complex I involvement in the two foundational COA6 cases; both have complex IV deficiency.

evidence.snippet: However, at this point, the question as to how a loss of COA6 affects complex I remain open as no link between copper chaperone activity and complex I biogenesis has been observed.
evidence.explanation: The 2020 investigators explicitly leave the mechanism of complex I involvement unresolved.

open_questions/2.rationale: The original patient had combined complex I/IV deficiency in heart and normal fibroblast activities, whereas the W66R patient had isolated complex IV deficiency. Engineered human cell studies also differ in complex I involvement. These observations establish heterogeneity; they do not make combined deficiency incompatible with COA6 disease. Genotype, tissue and culture conditions are candidate explanations, but their contributions have not been resolved.

evidence.snippet: All mutations have been found in Cockayne syndrome gene, CSB, xeroderma pigmentosum genes, XPD and XPG and ERCC1 gene involved in the transcription-coupled NER pathway.
evidence.explanation: Review enumerates the four causal NER genes whose biallelic loss-of-function produces COFS.

evidence.snippet: Deficiencies in NER typically result in a group of heterogeneous distinct disorders ranging from the mild UV sensitive syndrome to the cancer-prone xeroderma pigmentosum and the neurodevelopmental/progeroid conditions trichothiodystrophy, Cockayne syndrome and cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal-syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Positions NER-gene deficiency as the root molecular cause of COFS within the NER-disorder spectrum.

steps/4.description: Biallelic pathogenic loss-of-function variants in one of four NER genes (ERCC6/CSB, ERCC2/XPD, ERCC5/XPG, or ERCC1) eliminate or destabilise the protein product, removing its contribution to transcription-coupled NER. COFS represents the severe prenatal-onset end of the NER-deficiency allelic spectrum.

evidence.snippet: In COFS syndrome, as in Cockayne syndrome, DNA repair is impaired in the transcription-coupled NER pathway, but not in the global genome NER pathway.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the TC-NER-specific defect that mechanistically defines COFS.

evidence.snippet: Transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair is a specialized DNA repair pathway that helps to mitigate damage induced by 'bulky' adducts such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers and monoadducts formed by reactive oxygen species.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistic review describes the TC-NER pathway whose impairment is the proximal molecular lesion in COFS.

steps/5.description: The TC-NER complex (CSA/CSB → UVSSA-USP7 → TFIIH-XPD → XPG → ERCC1-XPF) is impaired when any required component is missing or destabilised. Damage in actively transcribed DNA can no longer be efficiently removed. COFS shares this defect with Cockayne syndrome (see Cockayne_Syndrome.yaml); the shared biology is mirrored here rather than inherited via `conforms_to` because dismech modules are reserved for cross-disorder conserved mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: Neural progenitor cells and differentiating neurons in the developing forebrain sustain high transcriptional activity and metabolic demand and are therefore vulnerable to DNA damage.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistic review explains why neural progenitors and developing neurons are uniquely susceptible to unrepaired transcription-blocking lesions.

steps/6.description: Persistent unrepaired bulky DNA adducts and oxidative lesions stall RNA polymerase II on the template strand of actively transcribed genes, preventing transcription elongation. The high transcriptional demand of neural progenitors and developing neurons makes these cells especially vulnerable.

evidence.snippet: TC-NER safeguards genome integrity and plays an essential role in neuronal differentiation, synaptogenesis, and neurogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistic review establishes the essential role of TC-NER in neuronal differentiation and neurogenesis, the developmental process impaired in COFS.

steps/7.description: Transcriptional arrest in proliferating neural progenitors impairs neuronal differentiation and neurogenesis, reducing neuron production. This developmental arm produces the microcephaly and cerebellar hypoplasia of COFS.

evidence.snippet: Impaired TC-NER pathway activity manifests in tissue-level pathologies, including neurodegeneration and increased susceptibility to neurological deficits.
evidence.explanation: Direct mechanistic link from impaired TC-NER to the neurodegenerative tissue-level outcome characteristic of COFS.

steps/8.description: Transcriptional arrest in post-mitotic neurons drives progressive neurodegeneration of surviving neurons. This degenerative arm contributes to the severe progressive psychomotor decline of COFS, distinct from the developmental neurogenesis deficit.

evidence.snippet: Cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal (COFS) syndrome is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder characterized by congenital microcephaly, congenital cataracts and/or microphthalmia, arthrogryposis, severe developmental delay, severe postnatal growth failure and facial dysmorphism with prominent nasal root and/or overhanging upper lip.
evidence.explanation: Foundational COFS review lists congenital microcephaly as a cardinal feature.

evidence.snippet: Microencephaly is present in the three fetuses with delayed development of the gyri, but normal microscopic anatomy at the supratentorial level.
evidence.explanation: Direct fetal pathology evidence of microcephaly in COFS pregnancies.

steps/9.description: Congenital, prenatal-onset microcephaly with markedly reduced head circumference, present in fetuses and at birth.

evidence.snippet: Cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal syndrome (COFS) is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease belonging to the family of DNA repair disorders, characterized by microcephaly, congenital cataracts, facial dysmorphism and arthrogryposis.
evidence.explanation: Defining clinical feature listed in the review of three fetal COFS cases.

evidence.snippet: Cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal (COFS) syndrome is a recessively inherited rapidly progressive neurologic disorder leading to brain atrophy, with calcifications, cataracts, microcornea, optic atrophy, progressive joint contractures, and growth failure.
evidence.explanation: Classical XPD-mutated COFS case series enumerates ocular features.

steps/10.description: Bilateral congenital cataracts, often with microphthalmia, microcornea, and optic atrophy. A defining ocular feature of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal (COFS) syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by microcephaly, congenital cataracts, facial dysmorphism, neurogenic arthrogryposis, growth failure and severe psychomotor retardation.
evidence.explanation: ERCC6 Finnish founder cohort documents neurogenic arthrogryposis as a cardinal feature.

evidence.snippet: We report on a family with five fetuses conceived to first cousin parents presenting with abnormal ultrasound findings including contractures and microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: ERCC5-truncating family with prenatally diagnosed contractures supports the prenatal-onset joint pathology.

evidence.snippet: COFS syndrome is characterized by very severe prenatal developmental anomalies (arthrogryposis and microphthalmia).
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies arthrogryposis as a defining prenatal anomaly of the COFS end of the Cockayne syndrome spectrum.

steps/11.description: Congenital, often prenatal-onset multiple joint contractures with a neurogenic basis, frequently detected on antenatal ultrasound.

evidence.snippet: Cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal (COFS) syndrome is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder characterized by congenital microcephaly, congenital cataracts and/or microphthalmia, arthrogryposis, severe developmental delay, severe postnatal growth failure and facial dysmorphism with prominent nasal root and/or overhanging upper lip.

evidence.snippet: COFS syndrome should be considered in fetuses when intrauterine growth retardation is associated with microcephaly, arthrogryposis and ocular anomalies.
evidence.explanation: Prenatal review highlights IUGR as a diagnostic feature alongside microcephaly and arthrogryposis.

steps/12.description: Severe prenatal and postnatal growth failure with intrauterine growth retardation and failure to thrive in survivors.

evidence.snippet: Cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal (COFS) syndrome is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder characterized by congenital microcephaly, congenital cataracts and/or microphthalmia, arthrogryposis, severe developmental delay, severe postnatal growth failure and facial dysmorphism with prominent nasal root and/or overhanging upper lip.
evidence.explanation: Microphthalmia is listed among the defining ocular anomalies in the cardinal feature set.

steps/13.description: Reduced ocular globe size frequently co-occurring with congenital cataracts, microcornea, and optic atrophy.

evidence.snippet: This syndrome is now recognized as a disorder belonging to the spectrum of inherited defects in Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) resulting in profound photosensitivity.
evidence.explanation: Review explicitly links COFS to profound photosensitivity via the underlying NER defect.

evidence.snippet: He presented with profound microcephaly, psychomotor retardation, failure to thrive, cutaneous photosensitivity, a bilateral hearing deficit and optic atrophy, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent episodes of pneumonia.
evidence.explanation: ERCC2-Gly47Arg case report documents cutaneous photosensitivity as a clinical feature.

steps/14.description: Increased skin sensitivity to ultraviolet light, reflecting the underlying NER deficiency. Severity varies with the specific NER gene defect.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar hypoplasia and ventriculomegaly were also present in two and fetal edema developed in the one fetus that survived beyond 24 weeks of gestation.
evidence.explanation: ERCC5-truncating family with prenatally diagnosed cerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: Microscopic anomalies reminiscent of pontocerebellar hypoplasia are present at the infratentorial level.

steps/15.description: Hypoplastic cerebellum with infratentorial microscopic anomalies reminiscent of pontocerebellar hypoplasia. Frequently visible on prenatal ultrasound when COFS is detected in utero.

evidence.snippet: Cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal (COFS) syndrome is a recessively inherited rapidly progressive neurologic disorder leading to brain atrophy, with calcifications, cataracts, microcornea, optic atrophy, progressive joint contractures, and growth failure.
evidence.explanation: XPD-mutated COFS case series lists optic atrophy among defining ocular features.

evidence.snippet: He presented with profound microcephaly, psychomotor retardation, failure to thrive, cutaneous photosensitivity, a bilateral hearing deficit and optic atrophy, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent episodes of pneumonia.
evidence.explanation: ERCC2-Gly47Arg case documents optic atrophy alongside other cardinal features.

steps/16.description: Optic nerve atrophy is a recognised ocular finding in COFS syndrome, reported in case series of XPD- and ERCC2-mutated patients.

evidence.snippet: This patient was documented as having a profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss at the age of 2 years.

evidence.explanation: Provides mechanistic basis for the sensorineural classification — direct histologic evidence of cochlear nerve degeneration in COFS.

evidence.snippet: He presented with profound microcephaly, psychomotor retardation, failure to thrive, cutaneous photosensitivity, a bilateral hearing deficit and optic atrophy, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent episodes of pneumonia.
evidence.explanation: ERCC2-Gly47Arg COFS case documents bilateral hearing deficit alongside other cardinal features (concordant with sensorineural classification from PMID:11300264).

steps/17.description: Profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss in COFS, with histopathologic evidence of accelerated cochlear nerve degeneration (axonal loss in the spiral lamina, complete absence of afferent fibers innervating inner hair cells). Reported in ERCC2/XPD-mutated patients and confirmed at autopsy.

evidence.snippet: Cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal (COFS) syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by microcephaly, congenital cataracts, facial dysmorphism, neurogenic arthrogryposis, growth failure and severe psychomotor retardation.
evidence.explanation: ERCC6 founder cohort lists severe psychomotor retardation among defining features.

evidence.snippet: Patient cells showed moderate hypersensitivity to ultraviolet rays and mitomycin C, yet the clinical features were very severe and, unexpectedly, were compatible with a diagnosis of cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal syndrome.

steps/18.description: Profound global developmental delay with progressive neurodegeneration typically leading to early death.

evidence.snippet: He presented with profound microcephaly, psychomotor retardation, failure to thrive, cutaneous photosensitivity, a bilateral hearing deficit and optic atrophy, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent episodes of pneumonia.

steps/5.description: Failure of hepatic ureagenesis causes systemic hyperammonemia. Ammonia is specifically neurotoxic and readily crosses the blood-brain barrier. evidence.snippet: The purpose of the study was to describe a pedigree with NEFL E396K mutation associated with a novel dominant intermediate Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (DI-CMT) phenotype.
evidence.explanation: The pedigree that established the CMTDIG designation and its causal variant.

evidence.snippet: Where the inheritance pattern of the mutations is known, it is always autosomal dominant for the in-frame deletion and missense mutations and autosomal recessive for the nonsense mutations located in the rod domain.
evidence.explanation: Separates the dominant missense alleles relevant to CMTDIG from the recessive null alleles, which cause a different disease.

steps/1.description: A single missense allele of NEFL, encoding neurofilament light polypeptide. Variants span the head, rod and tail domains, with recurrent hotspots at Pro8, Pro22 and Asn98; p.Glu396Lys, which lies just outside the rod domain and disrupts the heptad repeat that defines the coiled coil, is the variant reported in the pedigree on which the CMTDIG designation rests. ClinGen characterizes the pathogenic mechanism as a gain of function arising from misdistribution and aggregation of the protein — that is, the mutant subunit poisons the co-assembled network rather than simply being absent, which is consistent with the observation that heterozygous carriers of NEFL null alleles are unaffected.

evidence.snippet: In-vitro functional studies for all described variants depict disruptions in NF network and aggregation of NFL.
evidence.explanation: ClinGen's summary of the in vitro functional evidence across all curated dominant NEFL variants. Graded OTHER, not IN_VITRO: evidence_source classifies the cited publication, and a ClinGen curation record is a curation record throughout, whatever kind of study it is summarizing. INDIRECT for the same reason -- it reports somebody else's experiments.

evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemical analysis revealed multiple inclusions in the cell bodies and proximal axons of spinal cord neurons, disorganized processes in the cerebellum and abnormal processes in the cerebral cortex and pons.
evidence.explanation: Shows the aggregation in vivo, and shows it in central as well as peripheral neurons.

steps/2.description: Every CMTDIG-associated variant tested in vitro disrupts the neurofilament network and causes NFL to aggregate. In the Nefl N98S knock-in mouse the aggregates are visible as inclusions in the cell bodies and proximal axons of spinal cord neurons.

evidence.snippet: Electron microscopic analysis of sciatic nerves showed a reduction in the number of neurofilaments, an increase in the number of microtubules and a decrease in the axonal diameters.
evidence.explanation: Direct ultrastructural measurement of neurofilament loss from the peripheral axon and the accompanying loss of calibre.

steps/3.description: Neurofilaments are assembled in the cell body and delivered along the axon by microtubule-based transport. In the Nefl N98S mouse the sciatic nerve shows fewer neurofilaments, more microtubules, and smaller axons — the axonal content of the cytoskeleton is changed, not just its organization.

evidence.snippet: Neurofilaments are neuron-specific intermediate filaments essential for the radial growth of axons during development and the maintenance of the axonal diameter.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the normal function whose loss this node describes. Graded INDIRECT because it states the physiology rather than measuring the defect in CMTDIG patients.

evidence.snippet: A significant reduction in the sciatic nerve axon area, diameter, and G-ratio was also present as early as P21.
evidence.explanation: Measures reduced axonal calibre in a mouse carrying the murine equivalent of the CMTDIG variant p.Glu396Lys. Note the g-ratio falls together with axon diameter, meaning the axon shrank relative to its sheath; this is not a demyelination finding.

steps/4.description: Neurofilaments are the structures responsible for radial growth of axons during development and for maintaining axonal diameter afterwards. Losing them from the axon leaves a thin axon. This is the step that makes CMTDIG intermediate rather than axonal or demyelinating, and it has been measured directly in the mouse carrying the CMTDIG variant, where sciatic axon area and diameter are reduced from postnatal day 21 onward.

evidence.snippet: Electrophysiology showed uniform nerve conduction slowing in the intermediate range, both in distal and proximal nerve segments.
evidence.explanation: The electrophysiological finding that defines this entity, in the defining pedigree.

evidence.snippet: although intermediate forms of CMT with MNCV of 25-45 m/s are also recognised
evidence.explanation: Gives the conduction velocity band that defines the intermediate category.

evidence.snippet: However, it is important to note that axonal conduction velocity is also influenced by other factors including axonal caliber (Waxman 1980). Thus, a widespread reduction in axonal caliber could also result in a reduction in NCV.
evidence.explanation: States the interpretive argument that links the calibre node to the conduction node without invoking demyelination.

steps/5.description: Upper-limb motor conduction velocities fall in the intermediate band of roughly 25-45 m/s, in proximal as well as distal nerve segments, and this is what the CMTDIG label denotes. The important interpretive point is that a slow velocity is conventionally read as demyelination, but velocity also depends on axonal calibre — so a widespread reduction in calibre produces the same reading with normal myelin. NEFL is a neuronal protein and is not expressed in myelinating cells at all.

evidence.snippet: Their clinical picture was characterized by pes cavus, sensorimotor neuropathy and spastic gait. Both older patients showed ascending leg weakness to involve pelvic musculature.
evidence.explanation: The clinical syndrome in the defining CMTDIG pedigree.

evidence.snippet: Although the reduced velocities may well be mainly explained by preferential loss of large-myelinated fibres confirmed in 21 sural nerve biopsies
evidence.explanation: The nerve-biopsy correlate. Graded INDIRECT because the 21 biopsies come from NEFL-related CMT as a whole rather than from CMTDIG patients specifically.

evidence.snippet: We report the first nerve biopsy of a CMT patient with a de novo missense mutation in NEFL, and found an axonal pathology with axonal regeneration clusters and onion bulb formations.
evidence.explanation: Onion bulbs, the histological hallmark of demyelination and remyelination, appear in a nerve whose primary pathology is axonal and whose causal gene is not expressed by Schwann cells at all. This is the histological form of the entry's central claim: the myelin-range findings in NEFL neuropathy are secondary to the axon, not a primary Schwann-cell lesion.

steps/6.description: The clinical neuropathy: distal-predominant weakness, wasting and sensory loss with foot deformity, which in the more severely affected reported families ascends to involve pelvic musculature and produces a waddling gait. Sural nerve biopsies in NEFL-related CMT show preferential loss of large myelinated fibres.

steps/7.description: CMTDIG is not confined to the peripheral nerve. The route from NEFL aggregation to these findings is not established, which is why the edge into this node is typed as having unknown intermediates.

edges/5.description: Conduction velocity scales with axonal calibre, so a thin axon conducts slowly even with an intact myelin sheath.
