evidence.explanation: Primary septicemic (bloodstream/sepsis) plague occurred in 38% of this CDC human case series.

evidence.snippet: downregulation of genes such as thromobomodulin, which may play a role in coagulation, resulting in disseminated intravascular coagulation, a primary cause of death in plague infected hosts.
evidence.explanation: Human-monocyte data link Y. pestis-induced thrombomodulin downregulation to the disseminated intravascular coagulation that is a primary cause of death.

edges/0.description: Early immune evasion lets Y. pestis proliferate and disseminate into blood.

edges/1.description: Bloodstream Y. pestis infection triggers systemic inflammatory injury and clinical sepsis.

edges/2.description: Septicemic plague can produce coagulation failure with disseminated intravascular coagulation.

edges/3.description: Bloodstream Y. pestis infection manifests as sepsis in the septicemic form.

edges/4.description: The systemic proinflammatory response produces fever.

edges/5.description: Consumptive coagulopathy produces purpura and cutaneous hemorrhage.

evidence.snippet: In addition to aminoglycosides, other classes of antimicrobials including tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and sulfonamides are effective for plague treatment
evidence.explanation: Systematic review of individual treated human plague cases identifying several active antibiotic classes.

evidence.snippet: Mortality differed significantly among those receiving high-efficacy therapy (9%) and only limited-efficacy therapy (51%).
evidence.explanation: Surveillance analysis links prompt high-efficacy antimicrobial therapy to improved survival in reported U.S. plague cases.

treatments/0.description: Antimicrobial treatment must be started early because septicemic plague is a severe form of plague; aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and sulfonamides all have reported clinical activity in treated human plague.

evidence.snippet: The pituitary gland is enlarged as a result of lactotroph hyperplasia.
evidence.explanation: States the cellular basis of the pregnancy-associated enlargement modelled by this node.

evidence.snippet: The pituitary gland enlarges by about one-third to achieve these functional changes, with the major component of this growth being the estrogen-induced hyperplasia of the lactotroph cells.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the enlargement and attributes it to oestrogen-induced lactotroph hyperplasia.

evidence.snippet: The pituitary gland is enlarged markedly during 3rd trimester of pregnancy and reaches to its highest volume in the early postpartum days leading to increased demand of blood supply
evidence.explanation: Places the peak of the enlargement in the early postpartum days, which is exactly when the haemorrhagic insult occurs, and states the resulting increase in blood-supply demand.

steps/0.description: Rising oestrogen through gestation drives hyperplasia of the prolactin-secreting lactotrophs of the anterior lobe, so the gland enlarges substantially by term. This is normal physiology preparing for lactation, but it is the reason the anterior pituitary enters the peripartum period with an increased metabolic demand.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, small sella size may have an important contributing role in the etiopathogenesis of SS.
evidence.explanation: Case-control sella volumetry supporting fixed sellar volume as a predisposing anatomical factor.

evidence.snippet: The characteristic hook-shaped enhancement in Sheehan's syndrome well reflected the vulnerability to massive bleeding based on the complex pituitary vasculature, which has not been reported previously.
evidence.explanation: States that the pituitary's vascular architecture is what makes it vulnerable to massive bleeding.

evidence.snippet: Maternal gestational changes and adaptations include relative hyperplasia of the pituitary gland with minimal increase in blood supply to the hypothalamohypophyseal portal system due to increased blood flow being prioritized to reproductive organs.
evidence.explanation: States the mismatch this node models: the gland grows while its portal inflow does not keep pace.

evidence.snippet: Little changes in blood flow can lead to ischemia of the pituitary gland.
evidence.explanation: States the low perfusion reserve that is the substance of this node.

steps/1.description: The bulk of the anterior lobe is not supplied by direct arterial branches but by the long hypophyseal portal veins descending from the median eminence, whose tributaries arise far from the internal carotid artery; the posterior lobe and the marginal zone of the anterior lobe retain a more direct arterial supply. Because the whole gland is enclosed by the bony sella turcica, an enlarged gland in a small sella has little room to swell without further compromising this low-pressure inflow. Small sella volume is a documented predisposing factor.

evidence.snippet: None of them had clinical central diabetes insipidus.
evidence.explanation: In a cohort of 20 women with long-standing Sheehan syndrome, none had clinical diabetes insipidus, supporting relative posterior-lobe sparing.

evidence.snippet: Our findings demonstrated that patients with Sheehan's syndrome have an impairment of neurohypophyseal function.
evidence.explanation: Formal testing contradicts a strong reading of posterior-lobe sparing: neurohypophyseal function is measurably impaired even when patients are asymptomatic. Recorded as REFUTE against the absolute claim so the qualification in this node's description is auditable.

evidence.snippet: According to dehydration test, 8 (29.6%) patients had partial diabetes insipidus (PDI group) and 19 (70.3%) had normal response (non-DI group).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the sparing: about 70% of tested patients had a normal water-deprivation response and the remainder had only partial impairment.

steps/2.description: Because the neurohypophysis is supplied more directly than the portal-dependent anterior lobe, it is comparatively spared, and clinically overt central diabetes insipidus is not part of the usual presentation. The sparing is relative rather than absolute: formal water-deprivation testing detects partial neurohypophyseal impairment in a substantial minority of patients who have no symptoms of diabetes insipidus, and rare cases present with overt central diabetes insipidus.

evidence.snippet: Small sella turcica size, vasospasms (caused by PPH) and/or thrombosis (associated with pregnancy or coagulation disorders) are predisposing factors; autoimmunity might be involved in the progressive worsening of pituitary functions.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the haemodynamic and thrombotic contributors modelled by this node.

steps/3.description: Massive obstetric haemorrhage produces systemic hypovolaemia and hypotension; vasospasm of the hypothalamic portal vessels, and in some patients pregnancy-associated or inherited thrombotic tendency, further reduce inflow to the anterior lobe.

evidence.snippet: Sheehan syndrome is a rare but potentially fatal cause of hypopituitarism resulting from ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary following severe postpartum hemorrhage.
evidence.explanation: States the defining lesion modelled by this node.

steps/4.description: Sustained hypoperfusion of the portal-dependent anterior lobe produces ischaemic necrosis of the hormone-secreting cell populations. This is the defining lesion of the disease.

evidence.snippet: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed partial empty sella, supporting the diagnosis of SS.
evidence.explanation: Documents the empty sella as the chronic-phase imaging finding used to support the diagnosis. The corresponding imaging_findings entry records the radiological observation itself.

evidence.snippet: In the end, a fibrous scar replaces the necrotic pituitary by time leading to empty sella appearence radiologically.
evidence.explanation: States the tissue process, fibrous replacement of necrotic gland, that produces the empty sella modelled by this node.

steps/5.description: Over months to years the infarcted gland involutes, and cerebrospinal fluid fills the sella, producing the partial or complete empty sella seen on MRI in long-standing disease. This is a radiological consequence of the index infarct, not an independent lesion.

evidence.snippet: In accordance with the location of hormone-secreting cells relative to the vasculature, the secretion of growth hormone and prolactin is most commonly affected, followed by follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone; severe necrosis of the pituitary gland also affects the secretion of thyroid-stimulating hormone and adrenocorticotropic hormone.
evidence.explanation: States both the ordering of axis loss and its vascular-anatomical basis.

evidence.snippet: Multiple (≥ 2) hormone deficiencies were present in 68.8% of patients, with hypothyroidism (91.4%), hypocortisolism (88.3%), and growth hormone (GH) deficiency (85.7%) being the most common.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies multi-axis involvement in a 60-patient Sheehan syndrome cohort.

steps/6.description: Necrosis removes trophic hormone output in a characteristic order that tracks the position of each cell type relative to the vasculature: prolactin and growth hormone secretion are lost first and most often, then the gonadotropins, and only with more extensive necrosis thyroid-stimulating hormone and adrenocorticotropic hormone. Deficiency may be partial at presentation and accumulate over subsequent years.

evidence.snippet: None of the patients whose basal prolactin was below 4.0 ng/ml had adequate prolactin responses to TRH test, while all patients whose basal prolactin was above 7.8 ng/ml had adequate responses.
evidence.explanation: Documents deficient lactotroph reserve on dynamic testing in this cohort.

steps/7.description: Loss of lactotrophs abolishes the prolactin surge required to initiate lactation. Because it presents immediately after the index delivery, it is the earliest available clinical clue.

evidence.snippet: Somatotroph and thyrotroph cell loss occurs in almost all patients, with preservation or recovery of gonadotroph, lactotroph, and corticotroph cell function in few
evidence.explanation: States that somatotroph loss is near universal in Sheehan syndrome.

steps/8.description: Somatotroph loss occurs in nearly all patients and is unusually severe in Sheehan syndrome compared with hypopituitarism of other causes. It is the principal driver of the adverse body-composition, lipid and hepatic phenotype that persists even on adequate glucocorticoid and thyroid replacement.

evidence.snippet: A comprehensive endocrine evaluation revealed secondary adrenal insufficiency, central hypothyroidism, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, as evidenced by low levels of ACTH, cortisol, TSH, free T4, FSH, LH, and prolactin.
evidence.explanation: Documents biochemically confirmed hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in Sheehan syndrome.

steps/9.description: Loss of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone secretion prevents resumption of menstrual cycles after the puerperium and produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with loss of secondary sexual hair.

evidence.snippet: Laboratory investigations demonstrated microcytic hypochromic anemia, leukocytosis with neutrophilia, hyponatremia, markedly low morning cortisol (0.6 µg/dL), low FT3 and FT4, and low-normal TSH, consistent with panhypopituitarism.
evidence.explanation: The combination of low free thyroid hormones with a low-normal rather than elevated TSH is the biochemical signature of the central lesion modelled here.

steps/10.description: Thyrotroph loss removes the pituitary drive to the thyroid, so thyroid hormone synthesis falls without the compensatory rise in thyroid-stimulating hormone that characterises primary hypothyroidism. This node substitutes the disorder-specific lesion, central thyroid-stimulating hormone deficiency, for the module's generic impairment of thyroid hormone synthesis.

evidence.snippet: The major clinical features of typical and complete SS include lactation failure, failure of resumption of menstrual cycles after the puerperium, loss of pubic and axillary hair, symptoms of hypothyroidism, and hypocortisolism
evidence.explanation: Lists symptomatic hypothyroidism among the core clinical features of the disease, which is the peripheral consequence modelled here.

steps/11.description: Diminished circulating thyroid hormone lowers thyroid hormone action at peripheral target tissues, producing the hypometabolic symptom set shared with hypothyroidism of any cause.

evidence.snippet: It was found that 52.6% of patients had nonspecific complaints, 30.7% had complaints related to adrenal insufficiency, and 9.6% had complaints related to hypogonadism when diagnosed.
evidence.explanation: Nearly a third of this cohort presented with adrenal-insufficiency complaints, supporting corticotroph failure as a major clinical outcome.

steps/12.description: Corticotroph loss removes adrenocorticotropic hormone drive to the adrenal cortex. Because it usually requires more extensive necrosis, it appears later than prolactin and gonadotropin loss, but it is the deficiency that makes the disease lethal: an intercurrent illness in an unreplaced patient can precipitate adrenal crisis.

evidence.snippet: Symptoms are caused by a decrease or absence of one or more of the pituitary hormones, and vary, among others, from failure to lactate and nonspecific symptoms (such as fatigue) to severe adrenal crisis.
evidence.explanation: Names failure to lactate as a presenting manifestation of the hormone deficiency.

evidence.snippet: The major clinical features of typical and complete SS include lactation failure, failure of resumption of menstrual cycles after the puerperium, loss of pubic and axillary hair, symptoms of hypothyroidism, and hypocortisolism
evidence.explanation: Lists lactation failure first among the major clinical features, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/13.description: Inability to initiate breastfeeding after the index delivery, the earliest and most specific clue to the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: The major clinical features of typical and complete SS include lactation failure, failure of resumption of menstrual cycles after the puerperium, loss of pubic and axillary hair, symptoms of hypothyroidism, and hypocortisolism
evidence.explanation: Names failure to resume menses among the major clinical features.

steps/14.description: Failure of menstrual cycles to resume after the puerperium, due to gonadotropin deficiency.

evidence.snippet: The major clinical features of typical and complete SS include lactation failure, failure of resumption of menstrual cycles after the puerperium, loss of pubic and axillary hair, symptoms of hypothyroidism, and hypocortisolism
evidence.explanation: Names loss of pubic and axillary hair among the major clinical features.

steps/15.description: Loss of secondary sexual hair, reflecting combined gonadotropin and corticotropin deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Because symptoms often develop gradually and nonspecifically, diagnosis is frequently delayed until acute illness precipitates adrenal crisis or severe hypoglycemia.
evidence.explanation: States that acute illness precipitating adrenal crisis is a common route to diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: She developed an adrenal crisis during pregnancy, which was managed through hydrocortisone dose modification.
evidence.explanation: Documents an adrenal crisis occurring in a diagnosed and replaced patient under physiological stress.

steps/16.description: Acute, life-threatening decompensation of unreplaced or under-replaced cortisol deficiency, typically precipitated by intercurrent illness, infection, surgery or pregnancy. In a substantial minority of patients it is the event that finally prompts the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Laboratory investigations demonstrated microcytic hypochromic anemia, leukocytosis with neutrophilia, hyponatremia, markedly low morning cortisol (0.6 µg/dL), low FT3 and FT4, and low-normal TSH, consistent with panhypopituitarism.
evidence.explanation: Reports hyponatraemia in a patient presenting with Sheehan syndrome.

steps/17.description: Low serum sodium, a common laboratory finding at presentation and during adrenal decompensation.

evidence.snippet: A 48-year-old woman presented with central chest pain, productive cough, dyspnea, intermittent fever, severe anemia, and recurrent hypoglycemia.
evidence.explanation: Reports recurrent hypoglycaemia as a presenting feature.

steps/18.description: Recurrent hypoglycaemia, reflecting the loss of the counter-regulatory actions of cortisol and growth hormone.

evidence.snippet: SS presents with long-standing non-specific symptoms of fatigue and generalized body aches.
evidence.explanation: States that long-standing non-specific fatigue is the typical presentation.

evidence.snippet: It was found that 52.6% of patients had nonspecific complaints, 30.7% had complaints related to adrenal insufficiency, and 9.6% had complaints related to hypogonadism when diagnosed.
evidence.explanation: More than half of this cohort presented with non-specific complaints, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/19.description: Long-standing, non-specific fatigue and generalised body aches. This is the dominant symptom in the latent phase and the principal reason the diagnosis is missed.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals may present with signs and symptoms including weight gain or loss, cold intolerance, hair loss, menstrual irregularities, and hypotension.
evidence.explanation: Lists cold intolerance among the presenting features of the syndrome.

steps/20.description: Reduced tolerance of cold, a hypometabolic consequence of central hypothyroidism.

evidence.snippet: At a mean follow-up of 9.8 ± 6.8 years, NAFLD was present in 63% of patients, with 51% having severe steatosis, which was predicted by the presence of GH deficiency and higher body mass index.
evidence.explanation: Reports NAFLD in 63% of patients at long-term follow-up, supporting the FREQUENT band.

steps/21.description: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, frequently severe, attributed largely to untreated growth hormone deficiency.

evidence.snippet: The prevalence of MS in SS is around 50% with major constituents being increased WC, decreased HDL-C and increased TG.
evidence.explanation: States the prevalence of metabolic syndrome in Sheehan syndrome as around 50%, which is the basis for the FREQUENT band, and names its constituents.

steps/22.description: The composite metabolic syndrome is present in around half of patients, its dominant constituents being increased waist circumference, low high-density-lipoprotein cholesterol and raised triglycerides. Those constituents are curated separately below; this entry records the composite diagnosis and its reported prevalence.

evidence.snippet: patients with SS in comparison to age and gender matched population have increased body mass index (BMI) and total body fat with predominant abdominal fat deposition
evidence.explanation: States the increase in total body fat and its abdominal predominance relative to matched controls.

steps/23.description: Increased body mass index and total body fat with a predominantly abdominal distribution, which persists after thyroxine and glucocorticoid replacement.

evidence.snippet: Inspite of thyroxine and GC replacement, patients with SS have adverse lipid parameters like increased serum total cholesterol (TC), low density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglycerides (TG) and low high density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C).
evidence.explanation: Names each of the four lipid changes and states that they persist on thyroid and glucocorticoid replacement.

steps/24.description: A combined lipid abnormality - raised total cholesterol, low-density-lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides with low high-density-lipoprotein cholesterol - that persists despite adequate thyroxine and glucocorticoid replacement. The term is bound at the level of abnormal circulating lipid concentration because the claim spans changes in both directions, which no single narrower HPO term covers.

evidence.snippet: Homeostasis model assessment-insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), an index of IR was high in large group of women with SS compared to healthy controls
evidence.explanation: Reports HOMA-IR as high in women with Sheehan syndrome compared with healthy controls, which is the measurement behind this phenotype.

steps/25.description: Insulin resistance measured as an elevated homeostasis model assessment index relative to healthy controls.

evidence.snippet: Around one fourth of patients with SS had diabetes mellitus
evidence.explanation: Gives the approximately one-in-four figure that the OCCASIONAL band is taken from.

steps/26.description: Frank diabetes mellitus, reported in around a quarter of patients, alongside raised fasting and post-meal glucose values.

evidence.snippet: In another study including 60 patients with SS, osteopenia was found to be present 41.7 and osteoporosis in 35.0% of the patients and bone mineral density (BMD) was found to be significantly lower compared to the control group.
evidence.explanation: Reports osteoporosis in 35.0% of a 60-patient Sheehan syndrome cohort with bone mineral density significantly below matched controls, which is the basis for the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Sheehan syndrome increases the risk of osteoporosis and osteopenia
evidence.explanation: States the association between the disease and osteoporosis directly.

steps/27.description: Reduced bone mineral density progressing to osteoporosis, driven principally by the long period of untreated hypogonadism that the diagnostic delay creates, with contributions from the other unreplaced axes and from non-physiological glucocorticoid and thyroxine dosing.

evidence.snippet: The initial insult is caused by massive postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), leading to impaired blood supply to the pituitary gland, which has become enlarged during pregnancy.
evidence.explanation: Links the pregnancy-associated enlargement directly to the impaired blood supply that follows haemorrhage.

edges/0.description: An enlarged gland inside an unyielding sella and fed by a portal system has less perfusion reserve than a non-pregnant one.

evidence.snippet: Anatomically, blood supply to these unenhanced portions of the anterior lobe was via the hypophyseal long portal vein and trabecular artery, which are tributaries of the superior hypophyseal artery that originate far from the internal carotid artery.
evidence.explanation: Maps the non-perfused territory in acute Sheehan syndrome onto the portal-dependent vascular supply, supporting this edge specifically.

edges/1.description: The portal-dependent central anterior lobe is the territory that infarcts when perfusion pressure falls.

evidence.snippet: The pituitary stalk, majority of the marginal zone of the anterior lobe, the anterior lobe just in front of the posterior lobe, and posterior lobe were well enhanced.
evidence.explanation: Shows preserved posterior-lobe perfusion in the same gland and at the same time as the anterior infarct, which is the contrast this edge asserts.

edges/2.description: The posterior lobe, supplied more directly, remains enhanced when the portal-dependent anterior territory does not.

evidence.snippet: It is primarily caused by vasospasm of hypothalamic portal vessels following massive postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), resulting in complete or partial loss of anterior pituitary gland cells.
evidence.explanation: Names portal vasospasm after haemorrhage as the cause of anterior pituitary cell loss, which is exactly this edge.

edges/3.description: Loss of perfusion pressure across the portal supply is the proximate cause of anterior-lobe infarction.

evidence.snippet: Sheehan syndrome or postpartum hypopituitarism is a condition characterized by hypopituitarism due to necrosis of the pituitary gland.
evidence.explanation: States that the hypopituitarism is caused by the necrosis, which is the claim this edge makes.

edges/4.description: Destruction of the secretory cell populations removes their hormone output.

evidence.snippet: Follow-up MR image revealed marked atrophy of the anterior lobe.
evidence.explanation: Follow-up imaging in the same patient shows the infarcted lobe progressing to atrophy.

edges/5.description: The infarcted lobe involutes over months to years, leaving a partially or completely empty sella.

evidence.snippet: At a mean follow-up of 9.8 ± 6.8 years, NAFLD was present in 63% of patients, with 51% having severe steatosis, which was predicted by the presence of GH deficiency and higher body mass index.
evidence.explanation: Names GH deficiency as a predictor of steatosis in this cohort, which is the claim this edge makes.

edges/12.description: Growth hormone deficiency is a predictor of hepatic steatosis in Sheehan syndrome cohorts.

evidence.snippet: GH/IGF-1 deficiency appears to be the predominant contributor for abdominal obesity in such patients.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the abdominal obesity of these patients principally to GH/IGF-1 deficiency, which is the claim this edge makes.

edges/13.description: Growth hormone deficiency is named as the predominant contributor to the abdominal fat deposition that persists on other replacement.

evidence.snippet: These lipid abnormalities are attributed to persistent GHD
evidence.explanation: States the attribution of the lipid abnormalities to persistent growth hormone deficiency.

edges/14.description: The persistent adverse lipid profile is attributed to unreplaced growth hormone deficiency rather than to inadequate thyroid or glucocorticoid replacement.

evidence.snippet: Untreated GH deficiency (GHD) leading to IR, dyslipidemia and ED is the primary driver of increased CV mortality in hypopituitary subjects, who are adequately replaced with GC, thyroid and sex hormones
evidence.explanation: Names untreated growth hormone deficiency as what leads to insulin resistance in adequately replaced hypopituitary patients. The sentence is about hypopituitary subjects in general rather than Sheehan syndrome specifically, so this edge is INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES.

edges/15.description: Untreated growth hormone deficiency is described as driving insulin resistance in hypopituitary patients who are otherwise adequately replaced.

evidence.snippet: Most of these abnormalities are a consequence of GHD, GC therapy and hypogonadism, all these factors favour abdominal fat deposition and atherogenic dyslipidemia.
evidence.explanation: Names growth hormone deficiency first among the three contributors to the metabolic syndrome constituents, and names the other two, which is why this edge is not marked DIRECT.

edges/16.description: The composite metabolic syndrome is attributed jointly to growth hormone deficiency, glucocorticoid therapy and hypogonadism, so this edge carries only part of the causation.

evidence.snippet: Besides hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, other pituitary hormone deficiencies and inefficient or over replacement of deficient hormones all might play a role in the pathogenesis of decreased bone mass.
evidence.explanation: Places hypogonadotropic hypogonadism first in the pathogenesis of decreased bone mass while naming the co-contributors, which is why this edge is not marked DIRECT.

edges/19.description: The long untreated hypogonadism created by the diagnostic delay is the principal driver of bone loss, with the other unreplaced axes and non-physiological replacement dosing contributing.

edges/26.description: Cortisol deficiency impairs free-water excretion, producing hyponatraemia during decompensation.

edges/27.description: Insulin resistance with raised fasting and post-meal glucose progresses to frank diabetes in a substantial minority of patients.

evidence.snippet: Hormone replacement therapy is the only available management option so far.
evidence.explanation: States that replacement is the only available management, which is the claim this treatment entry makes.

evidence.snippet: She was started on lifelong hormone replacement therapy (HRT) consisting of hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, and estrogen.
evidence.explanation: Documents the composition of lifelong replacement in a treated patient.

treatments/0.description: There is no way to restore the infarcted gland, so management is lifelong replacement of the deficient target hormones, adjusted for stress and reviewed as further axes fail.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replacement supplies the target-gland hormones directly, bypassing the absent pituitary trophic drive.

evidence.snippet: The patient was started on oral glucocorticoid replacement with prednisolone 10 mg daily to address adrenal insufficiency, with plans for lifelong maintenance and stress-dose adjustments during periods of illness or surgery.
evidence.explanation: Documents lifelong glucocorticoid replacement with stress dosing in a patient with Sheehan syndrome.

evidence.snippet: glucocorticoid replacement should always precede thyroid hormone initiation in suspected or confirmed adrenal insufficiency to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis
evidence.explanation: States the sequencing rule that makes this treatment ordering-critical, and the harm it prevents.

evidence.snippet: Without appropriate steroid supplementation exogenously, patients can rapidly decline with adverse hypotension, altered mental status, and loss of vascular tone.
evidence.explanation: Describes the decompensation that follows interruption of glucocorticoid replacement, in a case where missed doses precipitated adrenal crisis.

evidence.snippet: This case demonstrates a secondary etiology of adrenal insufficiency, where the steroid regimen utilized glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid supplementation, but by understanding the pathophysiology, the mineralocorticoid supplementation was an additional and unnecessary course since physiological mineralocorticoid secretion is primarily influenced by adequate renal perfusion (i.e., renin-angiotensin pathway) and not directly associated with primary adrenal insufficiency
evidence.explanation: Supports restricting replacement to glucocorticoid: because the lesion is pituitary rather than adrenal, the mineralocorticoid axis is intact and fludrocortisone is not required.

treatments/1.description: Hydrocortisone replacement for secondary adrenal insufficiency, with stress dosing during illness, surgery and pregnancy. Critically, glucocorticoid must be started BEFORE thyroid hormone: correcting hypothyroidism first raises metabolic clearance of the little cortisol that remains and can precipitate an adrenal crisis.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Exogenous glucocorticoid replaces the cortisol the adrenal cortex no longer makes without corticotropin drive.

evidence.snippet: The patient was treated with glucocorticoid replacement therapy, followed by levothyroxine supplementation.
evidence.explanation: Documents levothyroxine replacement given after, not before, glucocorticoid.

treatments/2.description: Levothyroxine for central hypothyroidism, titrated on free thyroxine rather than thyroid-stimulating hormone because the pituitary feedback arm is the lesion. It must not be started before glucocorticoid replacement in a patient with suspected or confirmed adrenal insufficiency.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Exogenous thyroxine replaces the hormone the thyroid no longer makes without thyroid-stimulating hormone drive.

evidence.snippet: Pregnancy was later achieved through ovulation induction using human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) and human menopausal gonadotropin (HMG).
evidence.explanation: Shows that sex steroid replacement does not restore fertility, which requires gonadotropin therapy instead.

treatments/3.description: Oestrogen with progestogen for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism until the expected age of menopause, to relieve symptoms and limit bone loss. Fertility requires gonadotropin therapy rather than sex steroids.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Exogenous sex steroid replaces the ovarian output that absent gonadotropin drive no longer supports.

evidence.snippet: Replacement with GH in addition to standard hormone replacement improves their cardiometabolic profile.
evidence.explanation: States the benefit of adding growth hormone to standard replacement in this disease.

evidence.snippet: GH treatment had a favourable effect on CIMT, lipids and visceral fat.
evidence.explanation: Names the lipid and visceral-fat improvements that connect this treatment to the dyslipidemia and abdominal-obesity phenotypes it targets.

treatments/4.description: Recombinant growth hormone added to standard replacement in selected patients, which improves the cardiometabolic profile that persists on glucocorticoid, thyroid and sex steroid replacement alone.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Recombinant growth hormone replaces the absent somatotroph output.

evidence.snippet: AHAs were found in 8 out of 20 (40%) and APAs in 7 out of 20 (35%) patients with titers ranging from 1:32 to 1:128 and 1:16 to 1:32 respectively; however, in none of these positive patients AHA immunostained vasopressin cells.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the antibodies are present in a substantial minority of patients, which is the observation the open question is about.

evidence.snippet: Antibodies to unknown hypothalamic cells (releasing factor-secreting cells) other than APAs suggest that an autoimmune process involving both the hypothalamus and pituitary gland may contribute to late pituitary dysfunction in SS patients.
evidence.explanation: The authors themselves phrase the causal contribution as a suggestion inferred from an association, not a demonstrated mechanism, which is why this is curated as a knowledge gap rather than a causal edge.

evidence.snippet: Small sella turcica size, vasospasms (caused by PPH) and/or thrombosis (associated with pregnancy or coagulation disorders) are predisposing factors; autoimmunity might be involved in the progressive worsening of pituitary functions.
evidence.explanation: The primary review hedges the autoimmune contribution as "might be involved", in contrast to the predisposing factors it states outright.

evidence.snippet: The number of deficient hormones was found to be increased over the years.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the progressive hormone loss that any perpetuating mechanism, autoimmune or otherwise, would have to explain.

evidence.snippet: Following necrosis of the pituitary gland, autoimmunity may come to the scene either as a cause or consequence of development and deterioration of hypopituitarism
evidence.explanation: States the unresolved direction of the association explicitly, which is precisely the open question recorded here.

evidence.snippet: On the other hand, in a prospective study, 20 pregnant women with postpartum hemorrhage were followed up for 6 months and hypopituitarism developed in 25% of them and none of the patients were positive for pituitary antibodies
evidence.explanation: A prospective cohort in which post-haemorrhage hypopituitarism developed without any detectable pituitary antibodies argues against an obligatory autoimmune step, and is the main reason this is curated as an open question rather than a causal edge. Graded HUMAN_CLINICAL because the review is reporting the design and result of a prospective patient cohort here rather than offering an expert synthesis.

open_questions/0.rationale: Hormone deficiencies accumulate for years to decades after a single peripartum vascular insult, and a secondary autoimmune process against antigens released by the necrotic gland is the leading proposed explanation. Anti-pituitary antibodies are found in roughly a third of long-standing cases and anti-hypothalamus antibodies in about 40%, but these are cross-sectional associations in small cohorts with no demonstration that the antibodies precede the additional hormone loss or are pathogenic. Because the evidence does not establish direction, this entry does not draw a causal edge from autoimmunity to progressive hormone loss; the autoimmune contribution is recorded here as an open question instead. Resolving it matters clinically: if the process is active and antibody-mediated, antibody status might identify patients whose remaining axes are at risk, which nothing in current practice does.

evidence.snippet:
XRCC4 is indispensable for non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), the 
major pathway for repairing DNA double-strand breaks
evidence.explanation: Establishes XRCC4 as an essential NHEJ component, the function lost in disease.

evidence.snippet:
immunoglobulin levels are normal, and individuals 
lack overt signs of immunodeficiency
evidence.explanation: Although XRCC4 NHEJ deficiency impairs immunoglobulin junctional diversification, immunoglobulin levels remain normal and patients lack overt immunodeficiency — the differential developmental requirement for NHEJ proteins that distinguishes XRCC4 deficiency from SCID-causing NHEJ disorders (e.g. LIG4 syndrome), as asserted in the entry description.

steps/1.description: XRCC4 is indispensable for non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), the major pathway repairing DNA double-strand breaks, acting as the obligate binding partner of DNA ligase IV. Biallelic hypomorphic XRCC4 variants impair NHEJ and defective double-strand-break repair.

evidence.snippet:
XRCC4 deficiency leads to hypersensitivity to 
DSB-inducing agents and defective DSB repair, which results in increased cell 
death after exposure to genotoxic agents
evidence.explanation: Patient-cell studies show defective DSB repair and increased cell death, the cellular basis of genomic instability and impaired proliferation.

evidence.snippet: autosomal recessive mutations in XRCC4 induce increased genomic instability and cause a NHEJ-related syndrome defined by facial dysmorphism, primary microcephaly and short stature
evidence.explanation: Links XRCC4-driven genomic instability to the core clinical syndrome.
